etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English motif, from Anglo-Norman motif, Middle French motif, and their source, Late Latin motivum (“motive, moving cause”), neuter of motivus.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An idea or communication that makes one want to act, especially from spiritual sources; a divine prompting. [14th–17th c.]

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC, partition III, section 2, member 1, subsection ii:
quote.text: there's something in a woman beyond all human delight; a magnetic virtue, a charming quality, an occult and powerful motive.

definitions.definition: An incentive to act in a particular way; a reason or emotion that makes one want to do something; anything that prompts a choice of action. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1947, Malcolm Lowry, Under the Volcano, New York: Reynal & Hitchcock:
quote.text: Many of them at first seemed kind to him, but it turned out their motives were not entirely altruistic.

quote.citation: 2007, Joe Biden, Promises to Keep‎[1], New York: Random House, published 2008, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, page 110:
quote.text: “Your job here is to find the good things in your colleagues—the things their state saw—and not focus on the bad.”I said I understand.“And, Joe, never attack another man’s motive, because you don’t know his motive.”

definitions.definition: (obsolete, rare) A limb or other bodily organ that can move. [15th–17th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene v]:
quote.text: every joint and motive of her body

definitions.definition: (law) Something which causes someone to want to commit a crime; a reason for criminal behaviour. [from 18th c.]

quote.citation: 1931, Francis Beeding, “10/6”, in Death Walks in Eastrepps:
quote.text: “Why should Eldridge commit murder? […] There was only one possible motive—namely, he wished to avoid detection as James Selby of Anaconda Ltd. […]”

definitions.definition: (architecture, fine arts, music) Alternative form of motif
(transitive) To prompt or incite by a motive or motives; to move.
Causing motion; having power to move, or tending to move

quote.citation: 1658, Sir Thomas Browne, The Garden of Cyrus, Folio Society, published 2007, page 195:
quote.text: In the motive parts of animals may be discovered mutuall proportions; not only in those of Quadrupeds, but in the thigh-bone, legge, foot-bone, and claws of Birds.

definitions.definition: Relating to motion and/or to its cause

quote.citation: 1929, Arthur Lourié, “An Inquiry into Melody”, in Modern Music, volume VII, number 1, page 10:
quote.text: Debussy's melody is fractional, fragmentary. But at the core all his music is melodic and melody is its main motive force.
